headline: Why AI Coding Agents Slow Down & 5 Caching Fixes
summary: Extended AI coding sessions bog down as context windows bloat. Prompt caching reuses prior computations, keeping agents fast. Learn the mechanism, architecture, and five practical caching patterns to integrate into daily workflows.

slides.eyebrow: AI CODING AGENTS (E.G., GITHUB COPILOT, CURSOR, CLAUDE CODE) UPDATE
slides.title: Why Your AI Pair Programmer Gets Sluggish
slides.subtitle: Long sessions choke on accumulated context.
slides.body: Ever notice Copilot or Cursor dragging after an hour? The model re-reads every prior turn, bloating the context window. Prompt caching solves this by reusing earlier work.
slides.deep_dive: AI coding agents maintain a rolling conversation history. Each new request carries the full transcript — system prompt, file contents, prior edits, user messages. As the session grows, the context window fills, forcing the model to process more tokens per inference. Latency rises, costs climb, and relevance drops. Prompt caching identifies stable prefixes (system instructions, unchanged files) and stores their computed attention keys/values, so the model skips recomputation on repeat passes.
slides.key_fact: Context-window bloat is the primary cause of slowdown in extended AI coding sessions.
slides.why_it_matters: Uncached sessions waste compute on identical prefixes, degrading developer flow and increasing API costs.

slides.title: Prompt Caching: Reuse, Don't Recompute
slides.subtitle: Stable prefixes skip the attention computation.
slides.body: Caching stores attention keys/values for unchanged prompt segments. On subsequent calls, the model retrieves them instead of recalculating. Latency drops, throughput rises.
slides.deep_dive: When you send a prompt, the transformer computes attention over every token. If the first 80% (system prompt, repo map, unchanged files) stays identical across requests, that computation is pure waste. Prompt caching lets the server cache the KV cache for that prefix. Next request: the server concatenates cached KV states with new tokens, jumping straight to generation. Supported by major providers (Anthropic, OpenAI) via explicit cache-control headers or automatic prefix matching.
slides.key_fact: Prompt caching eliminates redundant attention computation for stable prompt prefixes.
slides.why_it_matters: Directly reduces per-request latency and token cost in long-running agent loops.
before_items: Higher token bills for repeated context

slides.title: How a Cached Request Flows
slides.subtitle: Cache hit skips prefix attention entirely.
slides.body: Request arrives → cache lookup → prefix match → reuse KV cache → append new tokens → generate. Miss falls back to full compute.
slides.deep_dive: The server hashes the prompt prefix (often first N tokens). On hit, it loads the precomputed key/value tensors from memory, concatenates them with fresh query projections for new tokens, and runs attention only over the suffix. This is analogous to memoizing a pure function: same input prefix → same intermediate state. Cache eviction policies (LRU, TTL) manage memory pressure. Developers control cacheability via `cache_control` breakpoints in the prompt.
slides.key_fact: Cache hit serves precomputed attention states; miss computes from scratch.
slides.why_it_matters: Understanding the flow lets you structure prompts for maximum cache hits.

slides.title: Editor → Agent → Index → LLM with Cache Layer
slides.subtitle: Cache sits between agent orchestrator and model.
slides.body: IDE sends context → local agent builds prompt → cache layer intercepts → LLM returns diff. Cache keyed on prompt prefix.
slides.deep_dive: The architecture inserts a caching proxy between the agent's prompt builder and the LLM endpoint. The agent assembles context: system prompt, repository map (AST index), open files, conversation history. Before calling the model, the proxy computes a prefix hash. If cached, it injects stored KV tensors into the model's attention layers. The repository map (code index) is a prime cache candidate — it changes only on file edits. The proxy also handles cache invalidation when the index updates.
slides.key_fact: Cache layer intercepts prompt, injects KV tensors on hit, falls through on miss.
slides.why_it_matters: Shows where caching lives in the toolchain — transparent to the developer.

slides.title: Developer Query → Structured Diff
slides.subtitle: Input flows through index, cache, model to artifact.
slides.body: Query + repo state → AST index builds context → cache checks prefix → model emits structured edit.
slides.deep_dive: The developer types a request ("add error handling to auth flow"). The local agent queries the AST index for relevant symbols, constructs a prompt with system instructions, repo map, and history. The cache proxy checks if the system+repo-map prefix matches a stored KV cache. On hit, the model receives precomputed attention for that prefix and only processes the new query tokens. Output is a structured diff (unified diff, JSON patch) applied directly in the editor. This loop repeats; each turn reuses the stable prefix.
slides.key_fact: AST index and system prompt form the stable cacheable prefix; only the query changes.
slides.why_it_matters: Reveals why repo-map stability is the lever for cache efficiency.

slides.title: Five Caching Patterns vs Common Pitfalls
slides.subtitle: Structure prompts for hits; avoid cache-busting habits.
slides.body: Pin system prompt, stabilize repo map, batch edits, version cache keys, monitor hit rate. Don't shuffle context, inject timestamps, or mutate prefixes.
slides.deep_dive: Pattern 1: Pin the system prompt at the very top — never modify it mid-session. Pattern 2: Keep the repository map (AST index) stable; only refresh on explicit file-save events. Pattern 3: Batch related edits into one request instead of many small turns — each turn extends the suffix, but the prefix stays cached. Pattern 4: Version cache keys with a hash of the repo map; invalidate only when the map changes. Pattern 5: Expose cache-hit metrics in your agent UI to debug misses. Pitfall: Adding timestamps or request IDs into the prefix busts the cache every turn. Pitfall: Reordering context sections changes the prefix hash. Pitfall: Including full file contents that change frequently — use symbol references instead.
slides.key_fact: Stable prefix ordering and content are the single biggest driver of cache hit rate.
slides.why_it_matters: Small prompt-structure changes yield large latency and cost savings.
items: Pin system prompt at top — never mutate
Stabilize repo map; refresh only on file save
Batch related edits into single turns
Version cache keys by repo-map hash
Monitor cache-hit rate in agent UI

slides.title: Integrate Caching Into Your Daily Loop
slides.subtitle: Three steps to faster, cheaper agent sessions.
slides.body: Enable cache in your IDE extension, structure prompts for stable prefixes, watch hit-rate dashboard. Flow stays fast for hours.
slides.deep_dive: Most modern AI coding extensions (Cursor, Copilot, Claude Code) already support prompt caching via provider APIs. Ensure your extension version is current. In your agent configuration, set `cache_control` breakpoints after the system prompt and repository map. Avoid putting dynamic content (timestamps, git SHAs, full file dumps) before those breakpoints. Add a small status indicator showing cache-hit percentage — if it drops below 80%, audit your prompt template. The payoff: sessions that stay snappy at hour four, not just minute one.
slides.key_fact: Prompt caching is natively supported by major providers; integration is often a config toggle.
slides.why_it_matters: Turns a hidden performance tax into a visible, controllable optimization.
takeaways: Update IDE extension; enable cache in settings
Place cache breakpoints after system prompt + repo map
Add cache-hit indicator; investigate drops below 80%
